section_summary: This section concludes the dispute over an Osaka Mainichi propaganda pamphlet that falsely attributed pro-Japanese remarks about North China to U.S. Military Attaché William C. Crane. Most of the section documents British diplomatic protests against Japanese military and postal interference with the Tsingtao Times, Peking and Tientsin Times, and other British newspapers circulating in North China. The correspondence traces the dispute from August 1938 through February 1939, ending with a Japanese denial of formal restrictions while acknowledging that newspapers might have been detained temporarily or mistaken for the banned Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2724 concerning false statements attributed to Lieutenant Colonel Crane
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that an Osaka Mainichi propaganda pamphlet falsely attributed pro-Japanese statements about North China to former Military Attaché William C. Crane.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that Crane categorically denied making the remarks attributed to him and that the story had attracted attention in Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Tokyo. Grew raised the matter informally with Foreign Minister Hirota, characterizing the publication as a violation of newspaper ethics and a gross injustice to Crane. Hirota promised to take appropriate steps, and Grew enclosed Crane's letter, a memorandum of his conversation with Hirota, and a South China Morning Post clipping.

subfiles.title: Crane's letter to the editor of the Osaka Mainichi
subfiles.about: Requests that the Osaka Mainichi omit comments falsely attributed to Crane concerning the restoration of order in North China.
subfiles.summary: Crane states that the Japan Advertiser had announced a forthcoming Osaka Mainichi holiday pamphlet containing supposed comments by him. He denies speaking to any press representative in Japan or North China about restoration of order and asks that the alleged comments not be published.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Grew's conversation with Foreign Minister Hirota
subfiles.about: Records Grew's informal protest over the publication of statements falsely attributed to Crane in the pamphlet Commonsense and the China Emergency.
subfiles.summary: Grew showed Hirota both the Osaka Mainichi pamphlet and Crane's earlier letter denying that he had made any statement about North China. He called the publication a flagrant disregard of newspaper ethics, a gross injustice to Crane, and propaganda likely distributed throughout the United States. Hirota read the quoted remarks carefully and promised appropriate action.

subfiles.title: Merry Christmas—Domei States the Case for Japan
subfiles.about: Describes a Domei holiday propaganda booklet defending Japan's conduct in China and quoting Crane and Franklin Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: The clipping reports that Domei circulated a Christmas booklet entitled Commonsense and the China Emergency, attacking Chinese warlords and Communism while denying Japanese territorial ambitions. It presents the pamphlet as an appeal against alleged misinformation about Japan. The booklet falsely quotes Crane as dismissing Chinese propaganda and invokes Roosevelt's quarantine language to argue that China should be isolated.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for General Araki's Japan Advertiser interview
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a despatch about General Araki's interview with Japan Advertiser representative Frank Hedges and the resulting difficulties and threats.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references Tokyo despatch no. 2798. It identifies the subject as a February 3, 1938 interview granted by General Araki to Frank Hedges of the Japan Advertiser, which subsequently led to difficulties and threats, with press clippings enclosed.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3253
subfiles.about: Summarizes British complaints about Japanese interference with the Tsingtao Times and Peking and Tientsin Times.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that Tokyo despatch no. 3253 enclosed British representations seeking protection for the Tsingtao Times and removal of the ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times. It characterizes the latter ban as serious interference with British rights and interests in North China. No Department of State action was considered necessary.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3253 transmitting British complaints about newspaper distribution
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits two British letters concerning Japanese interference with British newspapers published in North China.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards copies of letters dated September 15 and 19 from the British Ambassador to the Japanese Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs. Both concern Japanese restrictions on distributing British newspapers in North China.

subfiles.title: Craigie to Horinouchi concerning the Tsingtao Times
subfiles.about: Forwards the British Ambassador to China's account of interference with the Tsingtao Times and asks that further interference be prevented.
subfiles.summary: Craigie refers to Horinouchi's August 15 letter and supplies a copy of Archibald Clark Kerr's communication to Masayuki Tani. Kerr's letter describes continuing obstacles to distributing the Tsingtao Times and requests assurances protecting its employees.

subfiles.title: Clark Kerr to Tani concerning mistreatment of Tsingtao Times employees
subfiles.about: Disputes Japanese claims that interference with Tsingtao Times delivery had ceased and requests guarantees against further abuse.
subfiles.summary: Clark Kerr explains that the newspaper stopped using Chinese messengers because Japanese officials had provided no assurance of their safety. He states that four Japanese gendarmes, rather than local Chinese authorities, abducted a Chinese employee on May 17, held him for three days, and beat him. He asks Tani to secure assurances that such incidents will not recur.

subfiles.title: Craigie to Horinouchi protesting the ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times
subfiles.about: Requests the lifting of a Japanese ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times.
subfiles.summary: Craigie reports that Japanese authorities had banned the British newspaper and that censors were stopping even copies mailed first class to subscribers. The matter had been referred from the Japanese Embassy in Peking to Tokyo, with an unfavorable response anticipated. Craigie calls the ban serious interference with British rights and interests in North China.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3298
subfiles.about: Summarizes continued Japanese obstruction of the Peking and Tientsin Times despite British protests.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the ban had not been lifted and that postal workers had been instructed to reject copies addressed to individuals. It records that Tokyo despatch no. 3298 enclosed a British memorandum on the continued interference. No action was requested.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3298 transmitting a British memorandum on continued interference
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a British memorandum documenting continued Japanese interference with British newspaper distribution.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to his earlier despatch no. 3253 and transmits a September 28 memorandum from the British Embassy to the Japanese Foreign Office. The enclosure presents the continuing restrictions as interference with British rights and interests in North China.

subfiles.title: British Embassy memorandum on the continuing Peking and Tientsin Times ban
subfiles.about: States that the ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times remained in force and had expanded to copies addressed to diplomatic personnel.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum recalls Craigie's September 19 request that the ban be lifted. It reports no improvement and says postal employees had been ordered to refuse copies addressed to individuals in embassies and legations in Peking.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3413 transmitting further British communications
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a British note verbale reviewing the newspaper dispute and a formal protest to the Japanese Foreign Minister.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards two further British communications concerning Japanese interference with British newspaper distribution in North China. The first is an undated case history apparently delivered to the Vice-Minister on October 28. The second is Craigie's formal protest of November 2 to Foreign Minister Arita.

subfiles.title: British note verbale reviewing the Peking and Tientsin Times dispute
subfiles.about: Reviews unsuccessful British efforts to obtain the unconditional removal of the Peking and Tientsin Times ban.
subfiles.summary: The note recounts Craigie's letters, memorandum, and conversations with Horinouchi from September 19 through October 14. Horinouchi stated that local authorities would remove the ban only if the newspaper accepted conditions governing its future conduct, while Craigie insisted that an illegal and unfriendly ban should be lifted unconditionally. Although Japanese officials claimed that restrictions on copies for diplomatic and consular officials would be removed, postal authorities had received no such instructions. The note itself is undated but was apparently handed to the Vice-Minister on October 28, 1938.

subfiles.title: British formal protest against the Peking and Tientsin Times ban
subfiles.about: Formally protests the Japanese ban on the Peking and Tientsin Times and demands restoration of free circulation.
subfiles.summary: Craigie argues that the local authorities' action was beyond their powers, harmful to British-Japanese relations, and unsupported by any recent objectionable content in the newspaper. His Majesty's Government rejects the demand that the newspaper accept conditions before an unauthorized ban can be lifted. Craigie especially protests the continued interception of copies addressed to British diplomatic and consular officials and requests immediate removal of all restrictions.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3524 transmitting Dodds's letter on broader newspaper interference
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a further British communication about Japanese interference with newspapers in North China.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to despatch no. 3413 and forwards a December 2 letter from British Counsellor J. L. Dodds to Sho Kurihara. The enclosure reports that interference had continued and broadened beyond the Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Dodds to Kurihara concerning expanding interference with British newspapers
subfiles.about: Renews the demand to lift the Peking and Tientsin Times ban and reports detention of several other British newspapers at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: Dodds expresses surprise that the Japanese government had not acted on Britain's November 2 protest concerning the Peking and Tientsin Times. He reports that issues of the North China Daily News, Shanghai Times, and Shanghai Evening Post and Mercury dated November 5–19 were detained by the Tianjin postal administration, with most never delivered. He asks Kurihara to end both the original ban and wider interference with British newspapers in North China.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Tokyo despatch no. 3704
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Japanese response to British allegations that newspapers had been seized by the Tianjin postal administration.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the Japanese Foreign Office denied that the North China Daily News and Shanghai Times had been seized in November. It notes, however, that postal officials were cautioned because they might have confused those newspapers with the Peking and Tientsin Times.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 3704 transmitting the Japanese Foreign Office response
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a translated Japanese Foreign Office note responding to British complaints about newspaper restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Grew refers to his December 21 despatch on British protests over interference with newspaper distribution in North China. He encloses the February 10 Japanese note, which denies that special prohibitory restrictions had been imposed but says the attention of postal authorities had been drawn to the issue.

subfiles.title: Kurihara to Dodds denying formal restrictions on British newspapers
subfiles.about: Denies that the Tianjin postal administration formally prohibited the named British newspapers while conceding possible temporary detention or mistaken identification.
subfiles.summary: Kurihara reports that local inquiries found no special restrictions on mailing or distributing the North China Daily News, Shanghai Times, and other papers. He nevertheless acknowledges that copies might have been detained provisionally for containing prohibited propaganda or mistakenly confused with the Peking and Tientsin Times. He states that the matter had been brought to the attention of the postal authorities.
